newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila reaches out to opposition on new government.
newsitem.headline: Kabila reaches out to opposition on new government.

text.p: Self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila spent his first working day in Kinshasa on Wednesday with no sign that a promised government for his new Democratic Republic of Congo was in place.
"The people of Congo are still waiting for the government of public salvation," state radio, rebaptised the Voice of Congo, said at the start of its main evening news.
But in a positive sign of progress, Kabila's top aide met radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi in Kinshasa for talks on a new government.
Opposition officials said Deogratias Bugera, Secretary General of Kabila's AFDL alliance whose forces captured Kinshasa at the weekend, met Tshisekedi at the prime minister's office.

"They met for 55 minutes at the prime minister's office this afternoon," one opposition official said. "Tshisekedi came with proposals and Mr Bugera will be taking those proposals back to the AFDL leadership."

He added that efforts were continuing to bring Tshisekedi together with Kabila, who was leading consultations on Wednesday on a new administration to take over from the ousted regime of Zaire's veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
There was no indication that Thsisekedi, a populist politician sacked twice as prime minister by Mobutu, would be included in the government.
However, his fanatical followers from Kinshasa's teeming shantytowns expect him to be Kabila's prime minister.
A senior AFDL official said Kabila was meeting a broad range of people but dampened hope of a new government on Wednesday.
"I don't think there will be any announcement today. We are very, very busy. We re having meetings with many people," said the official who asked not to be named.
In the city of Kisangani students protested on Wednesday in one of the first signs of popular opposition to Kabila.
More than 24 hours after he flew into Kinshasa unannounced, Kabila was still cloistered with key associates in the official riverside residence of the prime minister.
Voice of Congo said "the President of the Republic" was only provisionally installed in the residence.
Aid workers in the northeastern city of Kisangani said more than 100 students protested peacefully against the alleged killing by a Kabila soldier of a fellow student.
They shouted "Tutsis go home", aid workers added.

France, a long-time friend of Mobutu, "solemnly" reminded Kabila that it was his duty to protect foreign nationals after two Frenchmen were shot dead in the capital on Tuesday but French ministers dismissed the killings as isolated incidents.
French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain meanwhile hinted that France might be prepared to admit Mobutu, who has cancer, for medical treatment.

World powers, both sympathetic and sceptical, have been pressing for a broad-based government as a sign of Kabila's democratic good faith and a first step towards multi-party elections. He had promised to unveil the government by Tuesday.
Kabila's forces took Kinshasa after a stunning seven-month campaign from the eastern border of the vast country.
They further consolidated their hold on the capital on Wednesday, when two senior general surrendered.

General Amela Lokima, military governor of Kinshasa and deputy armed forces chief-of-staff, and General Michel Elessi, commander of Mobutu's forces in the capital, turned up at a hotel and were taken away by security officials, witnesses said.

Mobutu, 66, remained in Togo's capital Lome after prolonging a technical stopover on health grounds. A source close to the government said he was "very weak" on arrival on Sunday from his jungle palace in north Zaire.
"We hope he can get the treatment that any sick person deserves," Godfrain told Reuters in France.
